## Project Name: ViewFinder
**Project Synopsis:** ViewFinder is a community web platform where users discover, share, and explore scenic viewpoints through an interactive map and geotagged photos.
# Sprint 1 Overview
Sprint 1 delivers a deployed, mobile friendly ViewFinder site where a visitor can see viewpoints on a map, open their details, and a registered user can log in and submit a new viewpoint. This sprint covers requirements 1–8 from the Initial Requirements Stack, totaling 40 story points over the first two weeks.

**Definition of** **Completion for Sprint 1:** Sprint 1 is complete when all eight requirements above work on the deployed site, each requirement meets every acceptance criterion in its artifact below, and its supporting evidence has been submitted. It is also complete when all Sprint 1 code is merged into the main branch.

**Working assumptions (proposed tech stack):** React (Vite) front end, Leaflet with OpenStreetMap tiles for the map, a Node/Express REST API, PostgreSQL for data, and cloud object storage for photos. Hosting is a free-tier web host with a public URL. The artifacts are written so they can be verified from a browser alone, regardless of final tool choices.

# Sprint 1 Architecture
ViewFinder is a three-tier web application: a browser based single page application, a stateless REST API, and two stores, a relational database for data and object storage for photos. Sprint 1 builds the thinnest working slice through all three tiers, so every later sprint adds features to a deployed system instead of integrating late.
## Component view
The React single-page app (SPA) is the only thing a visitor loads. It holds the five UI modules built in Sprint 1: the Map View (requirements 2 and 5), the List View (requirement 4), the Detail View (requirement 6), the Auth Forms (requirement 7) and the Upload Form (requirement 8). One responsive stylesheet (requirement 3) is shared by all of them. The map uses Leaflet and pulls base tiles from

OpenStreetMap, an external service, so the team hosts no map data. Every data request goes to the Express API as JSON over HTTPS. The API has three route groups, Auth, Viewpoints and Photos, each calling a thin service layer so the routes stay small and testable. Middleware checks a JSON Web Token (JWT) on every route that changes data, while reading viewpoints stays public. The API reads and writes PostgreSQL for users, viewpoints and photo records, and keeps the image files in object storage, saving only each file's URL in the database. The SPA and API are deployed to a public host (requirement 1), and the database and storage are managed services reached through environment variables, so no secrets live in the code.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 1. The browser talks only to the API, and the API alone touches the database and photo storage.
## Interaction view
The sequence diagram shows the most important Sprint 1 interaction, a registered user logging in and uploading a viewpoint, since this touches every tier. The user submits credentials, and then the API compares them with a salted password hash and returns a JWT, which the SPA keeps in memory and sends in the Authorization header. When the user submits the upload form, the API checks the token, stores the photo, and inserts a Viewpoint row with the title, text description, coordinates, and photo URL. It returns the new viewpoint, and the SPA adds a pin to the map and an entry to the list without reloading the page.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 2. The API verifies the token before it writes the photo or the database row. Dashed arrows are replies.
## Data view
Sprint 1 needs three tables: User, Viewpoint and Photo. A User has an id, a unique email, a display name, a password hash, and a created date. A Viewpoint belongs to one User, its creator, and has a title, a description, decimal latitude and longitude, and a created date. A Photo belongs to one Viewpoint and stores the image URL, its display order, and an upload date. A Viewpoint can have many Photos, although Sprint 1 only needs one, so the later gallery needs no database change. Later sprints add Review, Favorite, Report, and Category without altering these three classes' core fields.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 3. The Sprint 1 data model. PK is a primary key and FK a foreign key.
# Requirement 1: Publicly accessible web application (8 pts, priority 1)
**Requirement:** The application must be publicly accessible via a web browser.

**User story:** As a visitor, I want to open ViewFinder from any browser at a public URL, with no install and no login, so I can start browsing scenic viewpoints.
## Acceptance criteria
1. The app is deployed at a public HTTPS URL, written in the README and in the submission.

2. The home page opens without logging in, in the latest Chrome, Firefox and Safari, with no errors in the browser console on first load.

3. The deployed front end talks to the deployed API. The browser's network tab shows no requests to localhost`.`

4. The database and photo storage are hosted services. Data created before a redeploy is still there after it.

5. The README lists the steps to deploy from the main branch, and a teammate who did not write them can follow them.

6. The home page is usable (map visible, controls responding) within 5 seconds on a normal home connection.

# Requirement 2: Interactive map with geotagged pins (8 pts, priority 3)
**Requirement:** The main landing view contains an interactive map displaying geotagged view pins.

**User story:** As a visitor, I want the first screen to be a map of scenic viewpoints I can pan and zoom, so I can see where the spots are.
## Acceptance criteria
1. The map fills the main area of the landing view and shows OpenStreetMap tiles with the required attribution text visible.

2. The user can pan (mouse drag or touch drag) and zoom (scroll wheel, pinch, and onscreen + / − buttons).

3. Each viewpoint in the database appears as one pin at its stored latitude and longitude.

4. Pins are loaded from the API and are not hardcoded in the front end.

5. At least 5 sample viewpoints exist in the deployed database so the map can be tested. (The full seeding script is requirement 17 in a later sprint.)

6. A viewpoint created through the upload form (requirement 8) appears as a new pin after the page is refreshed, and immediately without a refresh when the upload succeeds.

7. If there are no viewpoints, the map still loads with no pins and no error message.

8. If the API request fails, the map still loads and a short "Could not load viewpoints" message is shown.

**Depends** **on:** requirement 1 (deployment). Requirement 8 supplies new pins.

# Requirement 3: Responsive design (5 pts, priority 2)
**Requirement:** Responsive design supporting both desktop and mobile viewports.

**User story:** As a visitor on a phone or a laptop, I want the site to fit my screen, so I can use every feature without zooming or sideways scrolling.
## Acceptance criteria
1. The page includes a viewport meta tag, and styles are written mobile-first with breakpoints.

2. At 1280 px wide or more (desktop), the map and the viewpoint list sit side by side.

3. At 768 px (tablet) the layout stays usable with no overlapping or cut-off elements.

4. At 375 px (phone) the layout is a single column, the list is collapsed or below the map, and there is no horizontal scrolling on any page.

5. Buttons and links on a phone are at least 44 × 44 px, and body text is at least 16 px.

6. The map works by touch: one-finger drag pans and two-finger pinch zooms, and the page does not scroll while the map is dragged.

7. Every Sprint 1 screen (map, list, summary card, detail view, login, register, profile, upload form) meets criteria 4–6.

**Depends** **on:** requirements 2 and 4 provide the map and list layouts; this requirement applies to every Sprint 1 screen.
# Requirement 4: List view of viewpoints (3 pts, priority 4)
**Requirement:** User can view a side-by-side or collapsible list view of all scenic viewpoints.

**User story:** As a visitor, I want a list of all viewpoints next to the map, so I can scan the spots without hunting for pins.
## Acceptance criteria
1. The list shows every viewpoint returned by GET /api`/`viewpoints , one entry each, with a thumbnail, the title and the first 100 characters of the description. If a viewpoint has no photo, a placeholder image is shown.

2. On desktop the list is a side panel next to the map. On a phone it is collapsed by default and opens with a visible "List" toggle button.

3. The toggle opens and closes the list, and the map resizes to use the freed space without distortion.

4. Selecting a list entry centers the map on that viewpoint's pin and opens its summary card (requirement 5).

5. The number of list entries always equals the number of map pins.

6. With no viewpoints, the list shows "No viewpoints yet" instead of a blank panel.

7. A long list scrolls inside the panel without scrolling the whole page.

**Depends** **on:** requirements 2 (map), 3 (layout breakpoints) and 5 (summary card).

# Requirement 5: Pin summary card (3 pts, priority 6)
**Requirement:** Clicking a map pin opens a summary card showing a thumbnail, title, distance, and an image.

**User story:** As a visitor, I want to click a pin and see a quick preview of the spot, so I can decide whether to open the full details.
## Acceptance criteria
1. Clicking or tapping a pin opens a summary card for that viewpoint within 1 second.

2. The card shows the photo (one image, used as both thumbnail and preview), the title, the distance, and a "View details" button.

3. Distance is the straight-line distance in miles from the user's browser location to the pin, shown to one decimal place (for example "12.4 mi"). It is calculated only if the user allows location access.

4. If the user blocks location access, or the browser cannot provide it, the card shows "Distance unavailable" and everything else still works. (The full "Near Me" search is requirement 11 in a later sprint.)

5. Clicking a different pin replaces the card. A close button, or clicking an empty part of the map, closes it.

6. The card fits a 375 px wide screen with no overflow and does not hide the zoom buttons.

7. "View details" opens the detail view for the same viewpoint (requirement 6).

**Depends** **on:** requirement 2 (pins) and requirement 6 (destination of "View details").
# Requirement 6: Detailed viewpoint view (3 pts, priority 7)
**Requirement:** A detailed view modal or page shows full-resolution photos, coordinates, and the description when a spot is clicked.

**User story:** As a visitor, I want to open a full page for a viewpoint, so I can see the photo at full size and read everything about the spot.
## Acceptance criteria
1. The detail view opens from the summary card's "View details" button and from the list.

2. It has its own address in the form /viewpoint/<id> . Opening that address directly, or refreshing, shows the same viewpoint.

3. It shows the full-resolution photo, the title, the coordinates as decimal latitude and longitude to five decimal places, the full description, the creator's display name and the date it was added.

4. The photo is the original uploaded file, not the thumbnail. The network tab shows the image loading from photo storage.

5. Formatting in the rich-text description (bold, italic, bullet lists) displays correctly.

6. A close button (or the browser's Back button) returns the user to the map at the same position and zoom.

7. An id that does not exist shows a "Viewpoint not found" message with a link back to the map.

8. The view fits a 375 px wide screen with no horizontal scrolling.

**Depends** **on:** requirements 2, 4 and 5 (entry points) and requirement 8 (a way to create content to display).
# Requirement 7: Secure user authentication (5 pts, priority 8)
**Requirement:** Secure user authentication allowing users to register, log in, and manage their profiles.

**User story:** As a visitor, I want to create an account and log in, so I can contribute viewpoints under my own name.
## Acceptance criteria
1. **Register:** a form collects email, display name and password. The email must be valid, the password at least 8 characters, and the display name 2–30 characters. A duplicate email is rejected with a clear message. Success logs the user in.

2. **Password storage:** passwords are saved only as salted hashes. No plain-text password appears in the database, the logs or any API response.

3. **Log in:** correct credentials return a signed token (JWT) and open the user's session. Wrong credentials show the same generic message, "Invalid email or password", whether the email or the password was wrong.

4. **Session:** the user stays logged in while moving around the app until they press Log out or the token expires. Log out removes the token.

5. **Profile:** a logged-in user can open a profile page, change their display name, and change their password by entering the current one first.

6. **Route protection:** the upload and profile pages send a logged-out user to the login page. API calls that change data return 401 Unauthorized without a valid token.

7. All authentication requests are sent over HTTPS.

**Depends** **on:** requirement 1 (HTTPS hosting). Requirement 8 depends on this one.
# Requirement 8: Photo upload form (5 pts, priority 9)
**Requirement:** An upload form allows users to submit personal photos with a title and text description.

**User story:** As a logged-in user, I want to submit a photo of a scenic spot with a title, description and location, so other people can find it on the map.
## Acceptance criteria
1. The upload page is available only to logged-in users. A logged-out user is redirected to login (requirement 7).

2. The form has these fields: photo file picker (required), title (required, up to 100 characters), rich-text description (required, with bold, italic and bulleted-list buttons), and latitude and longitude as decimal numbers (both required).

3. Latitude must be between −90 and 90 and longitude between −180 and 180. Anything else shows an error next to the field. (Clicking the map to place a pin and reading coordinates from photo data are requirements 9 and 10 in a later sprint.)

4. The file picker accepts only image files. A basic check blocks non-images in the browser. (Strict type and size rules are requirement 22 in a later sprint.)

5. Submitting with an empty required field shows a message next to that field and sends nothing.

6. On a valid submit, the photo goes to photo storage, and a viewpoint record is saved with the title, description, coordinates, photo URL and the logged-in user's id.

7. While the upload runs, the submit button is disabled and a progress indicator shows, so a double click cannot create two viewpoints.

8. On success the user sees a confirmation, and the new viewpoint appears on the map and in the list.

9. On failure (for example, the network drops) the user sees an error and keeps everything they typed.

**Depends** **on:** requirements 2, 4 and 6 (to display the result) and 7 (to log in).
